# The History of the Metric System

Before the late eighteenth century, measurement in Europe was a patchwork of local custom. A *pied* in Paris differed from a *pied* in Marseille; the *aune* used for cloth varied by trade and by town. France alone was thought to have some 250,000 distinct units in circulation. This was not merely inconvenient — it was a mechanism of exploitation. Feudal lords often controlled the physical standards, and enlarging the measure of grain owed in rent was a quiet form of taxation. When the *cahiers de doléances*, the lists of grievances compiled ahead of the Estates-General in 1789, were gathered, uniform measures were among the most common demands.

The French Revolution supplied both the motive and the authority to act. In 1790, Talleyrand proposed to the National Assembly a new system founded on nature rather than on the body of a king. The Academy of Sciences, with Lagrange, Laplace, Condorcet, and Borda among its members, took up the question. It made two decisions that shaped everything after. First, the system would be decimal, so that conversion between magnitudes required only shifting a decimal point. Second, its base unit of length would be derived from the Earth itself: one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator along the meridian through Paris. The name chosen, *mètre*, came from the Greek *metron*, a measure.

Fixing that length required knowing the meridian's length, and so the astronomers Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain were dispatched in 1792 to survey the arc from Dunkirk to Barcelona by triangulation.
